entries.name: Beaver dam
entries.purpose: pond creation; deepens a stream so the family can hide from predators and float food and building wood home
parts: food cache sunk off the dam
layout: spans a small stream, concave upstream
upstream face packed with mud to stop leaks
deep water upstream, shallow riffles downstream
entries.found: small forest streams with nearby woodland; a dam is topped up all season and can sit for decades
entries.notes: A family of four can raise about 1.5 m of dam wall a day. The record dam, in Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada, spans about 800 m and is visible from space; one 2003 estimate measured 400 m of beaver-cut canals feeding a pond.

entries.name: Beaver lodge
entries.purpose: family dwelling; dry bedroom above the waterline of the dam pond
layout: dome of piled sticks in the pond, no landward door
one or two underwater entrances on the lee side
chamber floor kept above water and straw-lined
entries.found: inside the dam pond; one or two lodges per family, repaired and raised as the pond level changes
entries.notes: Typically 3-4 m across, about 3 m high and built in around 20 days from some 3 tonnes of material. Entrances stay underwater, so the safe room has no door a predator can reach.

entries.name: Mound-building termite mound
entries.purpose: ventilated colony castle; stable climate for the fungus gardens that feed the colony
parts: nursery and queen cell at the base
layout: broad base tapering to turrets above a tall central chimney
cool moist lower chambers, warm fungus gardens above
outer wall sheds rain; flue walls are tuned all season
entries.found: warm, well-drained savannas and open woodland of Africa and southern Asia; mound density runs a few per hectare
entries.notes: M. bellicosus mounds regularly reach 4-5 m and the largest exceed 6-8 m high with 13 m-wide bases; some date back two millennia. The mound is the colony's lung: stale air out the top, fresh air in the base, near-constant 30 C inside.

entries.name: Coral reef
entries.purpose: colony housing and reef-wide ecosystem engineering; the living framework holds coral polyps and shelters a quarter of marine species
layout: grows in warm, shallow, clear salt water
crest toward the open sea, lagoon behind
built up over millennia; drowned reefs form banks and atoll rims
entries.found: tropical oceans between the tropics; the Great Barrier Reef off Queensland stretches about 2,300 km and is the largest animal-made structure on Earth
entries.notes: Hard corals lay down calcium carbonate at under a centimetre to several centimetres a year, so every block here is geological time. Reefs cover under 1% of the sea floor yet support roughly a quarter of all marine species.

entries.name: Red wood ant nest mound
entries.purpose: sun-warmed colony dome; solar heating for eggs and pupae and shelter for hundreds of thousands of workers
parts: brood chambers warmed by sun and workers
entrance holes on the dome flanks
layout: steep dome of needles piled over a soil core
south-facing slope picks up the sun
entrances on the sheltered side; trails run to tree crowns
entries.found: conifer and mixed forests of Eurasia, often in sunny clearings and forest edges; a mound can hold up to about two million ants
entries.notes: Domes can exceed 2 m high and 3-5 m across with 1-2 m of tunnelling beneath; Switzerland protects them, and foresters have used them as living biocontrol against defoliating caterpillars.

entries.name: Bald eagle aerie
entries.purpose: multi-use nesting and roosting platform; a fortress re-lined and re-used every year
parts: soft inner cup of grass, moss and lichens
sprig of green greenery added at incubation
layout: built high in the tallest tree near water, just below the crown
rimmed with soft lining cup in the centre
added to each season until it can weigh tonnes
entries.found: near lakes, rivers and coasts across North America; pairs rebuild the same nest for decades, sometimes until the tree gives way
entries.notes: Typical nests are 1.5-1.8 m across and under a metre deep, but the record Florida aerie measured 2.9 m across and 6.1 m deep and weighed about 2 tonnes; an Ohio pair used theirs for 34 years.

entries.name: Osprey nest platform
entries.purpose: fishing eyrie; open-top nest rebuilt high above water on snags, poles or cliffs
parts: soft lining of seaweed or sod
open crest facing the prevailing wind
layout: broad, shallow basket with a clear centre bowl
sited high with open flight access over water
often re-lined and piled higher year after year
entries.found: coasts, lakes and large rivers worldwide; artificial nest platforms are commonly adopted within a season
entries.notes: Ospreys dive feet-first for fish and nest almost anywhere with a clear runway. Man-made poles and platforms are now a standard conservation tool; one platform can host the same pair for decades.

entries.name: Wild honeybee colony nest
entries.purpose: brood rearing and winter food store; comb sheets hung in a hollow cavity
parts: brood cluster in the warm centre
honey and pollen stores at the edges
layout: several vertical combs spaced bee-width apart
queen and brood low in the cavity, honey high
entrance at the bottom edge, sealed with propolis
entries.found: hollow trees, rock fissures and building voids; feral colonies persist wherever hollow cavities and flowers overlap
entries.notes: A strong colony can hold tens of thousands of bees and survive winter on 15-30 kg of stored honey. Feral colonies carry the genes that keep managed stocks healthy, so wild nests matter beyond the honey.

entries.name: Barn swallow mud cup
entries.purpose: open-cup nest for aerial insect hunters; a plastered half-bowl under cover
parts: inner lining of feathers and straw
layout: plastered onto beams, eaves and bridge soffits under cover
open bowl facing inward along the beam
same site reused and re-plastered each spring
entries.found: almost everywhere people keep open-sided farm buildings and bridges; nests are often rebuilt in the same spot for generations
entries.notes: Built from hundreds of beakfuls of mud, one pellet per trip. Occupied nests mean healthy aerial insect life; sudden absence of swallows is an early sign that insect populations are crashing.

entries.name: Cliff swallow colony cluster
entries.purpose: communal cluster of jug-shaped gourds; safety in numbers and a mud-source beacon
parts: globular mud gourd with a side entrance
shared mud source below the colony
layout: gourds packed shoulder-to-shoulder under cliff overhangs or bridges
entrance faces outward and slightly down
colonies can hold hundreds of pairs on one wall
entries.found: vertical muddy cliffs, canyon walls, bridge culverts and dams where a muddy puddle and sheltered wall meet
entries.notes: Colony location advertises a good mud source to every passing swallow. Gourds are abandoned or reused yearly, and the same colony site can persist for a century; droppings below mark it from metres away.

entries.name: Sociable weaver commune nest
entries.purpose: communal apartment block; one thatched mass sheltering hundreds of birds through Kalahari heat and cold
parts: outer shell of thorny twigs against predators
layout: hung in camelthorn or other stout trees, also telephone poles
dome above, honeycomb of chambers below
chamber depth tuned for summer edge, winter core
entries.found: arid southern African savanna; one colony can shelter 100-500 birds in more than 250 chambers
entries.notes: Nests can exceed 7 m across, weigh over a tonne and persist for 100 years, so heavy trees collapse under them. Pygmy falcons nest inside abandoned chambers and depend on the weavers entirely.

entries.name: Baya weaver hanging nest
entries.purpose: swinging retort courtship nest; proof of skill to nest-inspecting females
parts: vertical entrance tube below the belly
layout: hangs vertically from fine branches over water or paddy
entrance is a long downward tube
males weave many nests; females accept only good craft
entries.found: Indian reed paddies, palms and acacia scrub; colonies of dozens of dangling nests sway over monsoon fields
entries.notes: A male may weave dozen(s) of nests photographed from afar like hanging figs; only sound construction earns a mate. The long entrance tube keeps rats and snakes out of the chamber.

entries.name: White stork rooftop nest
entries.purpose: large platform nest re-used as a skyline landmark; a village institution on the chimney neighbours watch over
layout: built on chimneys, telegraph poles and rooftops in village Europe and the Middle East
central shallow bowl above a wide stick pedestal
added to yearly, so nests can outweigh the chimney
entries.found: villages across central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East; famously spread on European rooftops after chimneys were stork-wired
entries.notes: One German site (Wehrsdorf) was documented as a continuous stork nest site from 1549 to 1930, about 381 years of repairs by successive pairs. Folklore counts the stork as the bringer of babies across Europe.

entries.name: Chimpanzee night nest
entries.purpose: one-night sleeping platform in a tree; made fresh every evening, abandoned by morning
layout: built 10-20 m up in rainforest trees, occasionally on the ground
mattress weave is tested with a sit before lights-out
old nests mark old travel routes
entries.found: African rainforest and woodland savanna; nest surveys are the standard way to census wild ape populations
entries.notes: Apes rebuild their nest every single night and show strong preferences for certain trees and slopes. Counting old and new nests is how most chimp censuses estimate how many animals a forest holds.

entries.name: Bowerbird bower
entries.purpose: courtship display arena; a stage a male builds, decorates and defends but never sleeps in
parts: collection of blue or coloured treasures
paint strokes on the avenue walls
layout: a narrow stick avenue with a cleared court before it
treasures sorted and re-sorted by colour
male displays inside the avenue while the female judges from the court
entries.found: Australian and New Guinean forests; males clear the same bower site for years and repaint it with chewed saliva and charcoal
entries.notes: This is not a nest but a dating arena, and it is closer to art than shelter. Satin bowerbirds steal each other's blue straws, so bowers leak treasures across the valley every season.

entries.name: Edible swiftlet nest
materials: a few feathers in darker nests
entries.purpose: cave nest moulded by the male; also a farmed delicacy harvested for bird's nest soup
parts: creamy cup glued to a cave wall
a few outer feathers in lower grades
layout: half-bowl cup glued to a vertical wall in caves or dark houses
one nest per pair per season; several harvests a year in farms
entries.found: Southeast and East Asia sea caves and purpose-built swiftlet houses; farmed in the millions of nests per year
entries.notes: The nest is nearly pure hardened saliva, piped out over weeks. Raw nests fetch hundreds of dollars per kilogram; over-harvesting has hollowed out wild cave colonies, so the farm trade now dominates.

entries.name: Malleefowl incubator mound
entries.purpose: geothermal incubator; a compost heap the male tunes daily for a month-long egg warm-up
parts: egg trench in the warm heart
layout: broad cone of layered litter up to 11 m across
male digs holes to check temperature with his beak
adds or removes sand as the compost heats or cools
entries.found: semi-arid mallee shrublands of southern Australia; old mounds scar the scrub for decades
entries.notes: Guinness measures up to 4.57 m tall and 10.6 m across, about 250 cubic metres and 300 tonnes of scratched-together litter. Chicks hatch fully feathered and walk off alone; the parents never meet them.

entries.name: Alligator mound nest
entries.purpose: solar and compost incubation; heat of rotting vegetation warms the egg clutch
parts: flattened top left by the nesting female
layout: mound heaped in marsh grass at the water edge
egg chamber hollowed mid-build then roofed with litter
female guards it from above until hatching
entries.found: freshwater marshes and slow rivers of the American southeast and Nile crocodile wetlands; one mound per year per female
entries.notes: Decomposition heats the chamber for about two months; hotter nests skew hatchlings male, cooler nests female in American alligators. The attending female answers her hatchlings' chirps by digging them out and carrying them to water.

entries.name: Flamingo mud nest
entries.purpose: flood-proof turret nest; keeps one egg above sudden lake level swings
parts: crusted footprint ring around the cone
layout: cones in dense gregarious colonies on shallow saline margins
crater holds a single chalky egg
birds stand on the crater rim facing the wind
entries.found: saline coastal and alkaline rift lakes; Camargue (France), Lake Natron (Tanzania) and the Andean altiplano host the great colonies
entries.notes: Both partners build and defend the cone; breaking the egg because the nest leans is a daily risk. Flamingo pink comes from algae and crustaceans, so colony colour maps directly to local food chemistry.

entries.name: Oyster reef
entries.purpose: living breakwater and water filter; generations cementing shell onto shell in estuaries
layout: bars and beds hugging estuary channels, oriented to the tidal flow
crest near low water, slopes into subtidal depths
entries.found: brackish estuaries on every temperate coast; Delaware Bay and Chesapeake Bay once held reefs hundreds of km long
entries.notes: A single oyster filters close to 190 litres of water a day, so reef beds clear whole estuaries. Intensive dredging reduced world oyster reefs to a small fraction of their pre-industrial extent; reef restoration is now a major conservation program.

entries.name: Glass sponge reef
entries.purpose: deep-sea reef built by sponges; living fossil frame sheltering rockfish nurseries
layout: deep cold shelf water 90-300 m down, some as shallow as 22 m
patches and reefs up to 25 m tall, hectares of seafloor
entries.found: British Columbia and Alaska coasts; the Hecate Strait reefs discovered in 1987 span about 1,000 km2 and are over 9,000 years old
entries.notes: Thought extinct since the Jurassic until 1987; they filter plankton and bacteria for over 120 other species. Bottom trawling shattered whole reefs, and they now sit inside marine protected areas regrowing at 1-2 cm a year.

entries.name: Paper wasp open comb
entries.purpose: open brood comb hung under cover; a few dozen workers hunting caterpillars for the nest
parts: single exposed comb of hex cells
cap of brood in the centre cells
layout: umbrella comb hung by a stalk from eaves, twigs or under railings
cells open-faced, no paper envelope
small colony; one foundress or a small sister group
entries.found: warm temperate gardens and farm buildings; abandoned by winter and collapsed by frost
entries.notes: A friend of gardeners: Polistes are caterpillar specialists. Open combs are easy to spot at doorways in spring and are best left alone unless someone is allergic, since they sting only when molested.

entries.name: Bald-faced hornet paper nest
entries.purpose: aerial fortress of stacked combs wrapped in a football-sized paper shell
parts: narrow entrance pore at the base
layout: hangs from a branch or fork by a single stalk
entrance at the bottom rim; combs suspended in air inside
nest grows top-down as combs are added
entries.found: temperate North American woodland edge and gardens; each nest is an annual, deserted by first frost
entries.notes: Really a large yellowjacket, despite the name. Hundreds of workers will defend the paper shell fiercely at close range; at a distance they are harmless hunters of flies. The grey swirl pattern is unmistakable in winter, when dead nests hang bare.

entries.name: Rabbit warren
entries.purpose: communal burrow city; generations of tunnels and breeding stops in soft ground
parts: nesting stops lined with hay and fur
layout: honeycomb of shallow burrows 1-3 m down in sandy rises
many entrances, several lookout stops per entrance
warren edges ringed with scratch piles and droppings
entries.found: soft dry grassland and dune country; famously destructive in Australia and New Zealand where rabbits have no predators
entries.notes: One warren can shelter dozens of rabbits and persist for decades; introduced European rabbits helped strip Australian grasslands and wiped out native grazers. Burrows double as homes for snakes, ferrets and burrowing owls.

entries.name: European badger sett
entries.purpose: multi-generational underground clan house; main sett plus satellite setts across the clan territory
parts: spoil mounds and worn entry ramps
layout: tunnels 1-4 m down with chambers under root protection
entrances fanned with spoil, bedding and hair
latrine pits mark the sett's boundary
entries.found: wooded country and farmland across Eurasia; a main sett can have dozens of holes and hundreds of metres of tunnel
entries.notes: Setts are inherited and extended for generations, some so old they slide into archaeology. Badgers drag fresh grass bedding underground weekly and air chambers in sunny weather; the bedding smell is a dead giveaway to trackers.

entries.name: Black-tailed prairie dog town
entries.purpose: burrow city on open grassland; coterie family units defending shared burrow networks
layout: burrow clusters across grazed short-grass prairie
rim-crater helps funnel rain away from the tunnel mouth
lookouts stand bolt upright beside crater rims
entries.found: North American shortgrass prairie; modern towns span a few km2, but a Texas town of the 1890s ran about 400 km by 160 km with some 400 million dogs
entries.notes: The historic Texas town between San Angelo and Clarendon covered nearly 65,000 km2. Prairie dogs are a keystone species: ferrets, burrowing owls, hawks and swift foxes all live inside their towns.

entries.name: Molehill
entries.purpose: spoil disposal from tunnelling; vented stack-marks above the burrow network
layout: hills appear in loose soil above fresh runs
runs follow earthworm country; mowing and rolling soon erase them
entries.found: lawns, meadows and pasture across temperate Eurasia; a single mole can push up hundreds of hills a year
entries.notes: The hill is the exhaust pipe of a meter-thick tunnelling machine. Mole runs aerate the soil and farmers once followed moles as free drainage planners; gardeners still curse the lawn aftermath.

entries.name: Spotted hyena communal den
entries.purpose: cub nursery; an enlarged burrow or termite mound the clan uses and rotates
layout: often dug into a disused aardvark burrow or a termite mound with a baked-hard wall
cubs raised communally; lairs switched every few weeks
entries.found: African savanna and open woodland; clans enlarge abandoned termite mounds into dens and move cubs between lairs
entries.notes: Hyena dens reek of bone and musk and mark territory. Den switching dodges parasites and predators; a den site abandoned for a year is usually collapsed and re-opened elsewhere nearby.

entries.name: Orb-weaver spider web
entries.purpose: flight-interception fishing net; rebuilt daily from recycled silk
layout: vertical wheel strung across flight paths in vegetation
hub offset to one side; spider waits at the hub or in a side retreat
entries.found: anywhere flying insects and anchor points overlap; dewy mornings outline every web in grass and hedgerows
entries.notes: Orb webs can span a metre across; by weight spider silk beats steel for strength. The spider eats its own web each morning to reclaim the protein, which is why undamaged webs vanish overnight.

entries.name: Trapdoor spider burrow
entries.purpose: silk-lined ambush shaft with a hinged, camouflaged door
parts: vertical shaft up to 60 cm deep
camouflage of soil and debris on the lid
layout: shaft bored straight into soft soil or a bank
lid swings on a silk hinge flush with the surface
spider emerges at night to snatch passing prey
entries.found: warm temperate and tropical dry country worldwide; some lineages reuse the same burrow lineage for generations
entries.notes: The door is a living turret lid that swings shut on a silk hinge and vanishes into the soil texture. Spiders can live for decades, and empty doors left in gardens confuse even experienced foragers.

entries.name: Antlion pitfall trap
entries.purpose: conical sand trap; the larva lies buried at the apex waiting for sliding ants
layout: cone dug in fine dry sand under eaves or rock overhangs
steep inner slope near angle of repose; every step inward slides
larva flicks sand at climbers to finish the avalanche
entries.found: dry sandy sheltered spots where fine dust accumulates; each pit holds one larva and is rebuilt after every rain
entries.notes: Pits are snow-cone shaped arithmetic: the steepest stable angle of loose sand. One flick from the larva turns a climbing ant into an avalanche down into waiting jaws.

entries.name: Salmon redd
entries.purpose: spawning nest dug into the streambed; an excavated cradle for eggs in flowing water
layout: fresh bright gravel patch against darker algae-stained bed
cut facing upstream; eggs laid in a hollow, then buried and sealed
entries.found: gravel-bottomed rivers and streams on every salmon-bearing continent; a single female may dig several redds
entries.notes: Redds read like pale scars on the riverbed and are a legally protected sight in salmon country. Eggs incubate for weeks to months in the gravel; timing to hatch depends on water temperature, not the calendar.

entries.name: Compass (magnetic) termite mound
entries.purpose: solar radiator mound; a blade aligned to soak up morning and evening sun
parts: thin wedge ridge oriented roughly north-south
moist tunnel core inside the ridge
layout: elongated blade up to 4-5 m tall, narrow north-south
faces east and west to catch low sun and avoid midday scorch
crest casts a knife-thin shadow at noon
entries.found: monsoonal savannas of northern Australia; mound fields dot river floodplains and open woodland
entries.notes: The steelworker's compass of the termite world: a 4 m wall pointing about true north. Long debunked as 'magnetic', the ridge is really a solar panel in wearable clay, balancing warmth and avoiding fatal noon heat.

entries.name: Pufferfish mystery circle
entries.purpose: sculptural courtship arena; a 2 m mandala built by a 10 cm fish to seduce one female
parts: outer ring of 25-30 deep radial ditches
layout: circle 10-30 m deep in sand off Amami-Oshima, Japan
two distinct zones: spoked outer rim, labyrinth core
male tends the ridges; eggs laid in the calm centre
entries.found: shallow sandy seabeds off southern Amami-Oshima Island; known to science since around 1995, builder identified only in 2011
entries.notes: A fish the size of a pear spends 7-9 days digging a 2 m circle with perfect symmetry. The ridges channel oxygen-rich currents into the nest, doubling as engineering and advertising.

entries.name: Octopus den and midden
entries.purpose: fortress lair; a rock pile the octopus evicts tenants from and armors with trash
layout: wedged under rocky ledges with one crab-sized way in
midden of discarded shells beside the entrance betrays occupation
octopus blocks the door with shells and rocks from inside
entries.found: rocky coasts worldwide; dens cluster in 'octopus gardens', with hundreds documented off California and Australia
entries.notes: A midden of scallop and crab shell is the calling card of an occupied den. Octopuses rearrange boulders and shells as daily barricades; dens are inherited, kitted out and re-fortified across generations.

entries.name: Caddisfly larval case
entries.purpose: portable armour house; a silk tube wearing local building materials
parts: head and legs emerging from one end
layout: case dragged along streambed; larva walks with it wherever it feeds
open ends top and bottom; head and legs at the front
entries.found: freshwater streams and ponds worldwide; every species has its signature mosaic of sand, sticks or leaf
entries.notes: Made of silk and whatever the stream supplies; a species can be identified from its case alone. Anglers imitate caddis husks with lures, and the insect order's name means 'hairy wings'.
